## Introduction
- Loss of gastric volume and function causes disorganization in the digestive system, leading to complex symptoms known as **postgastrectomy syndromes**.
- These syndromes impair quality of life and nutritional status.
- Can occur even without gastrectomy due to altered gastric function (e.g., dumping after pyloroplasty or fundoplication).
- Most patients have one or more of the following: diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and malnutrition/nutritional deficiency.

## Changing Landscape of Gastric Surgery
- Elective gastric surgery for peptic ulcer disease has virtually disappeared.
- Bariatric surgery has increased dramatically.
- Therapeutic vagotomy is rarely performed, but partial, complete, or inadvertent vagotomy still occurs during obesity and reflux surgeries.
- Laparoscopic fundoplication is the most common cause of dumping syndrome (DS) in children.
- Gastric cancer remains the 4th leading cause of cancer death worldwide, requiring gastrectomy with various reconstructions.

## The Physiological Function of the Stomach
- **Accommodation:** Adapts to large volumes of ingested liquids and solids via vagally mediated accommodation and receptive relaxation.
- **Secretion:** Secretes acid and digestive enzymes (pepsin) to convert hypertonic intragastric contents into isosmotic gastric chyme.
- **Absorption:** Gastric acid optimizes iron and calcium absorption. Intrinsic factor (from parietal cells) contributes to vitamin B12 absorption.
- **Hormones:** Ghrelin ("hunger hormone" from fundus cells) regulates appetite, food intake, energy metabolism, osteoblast proliferation, neurogenesis, and myogenesis.

## Vagal Control and GI Coordination
- Vagal nerves control organized gastric contraction and stimulate secretion of acid, enzymes, and hormones.
- Lower esophageal sphincter (LES) creates a high-pressure zone preventing reflux against the thoracoabdominal pressure gradient.
- Under vagal control, the pylorus relaxes to receive food and regulates gastric emptying in coordination with duodenal motility.
- **Antroduodenal coordination:** The duodenum relaxes during antral contractions.

## Consequences of Gastrectomy on GI Function
- **Subtotal/Total Gastrectomy:** Loss of gastric volume limits food intake; loss of pylorus causes rapid emptying of high-osmolar food (Dumping Syndrome).
- **Vagus Division/Duodenum Bypass:** Decreased pancreatic and biliary secretion, leading to biliary dyskinesia and pancreatic insufficiency.
- **Total Gastrectomy:** Loss of LES causes persistent esophageal alkaline reflux; loss of ghrelin causes loss of appetite.
- **Loss of Intrinsic Factor:** Prevents dietary vitamin B12 absorption, resulting in chronic anemia.
- **Roux-en-Y Reconstruction:** Food bypasses duodenum and proximal jejunum, causing malabsorption of vitamins and minerals (calcium, iron).

## Postoperative Nutritional Monitoring & Dietary Instructions
- Postgastrectomy syndromes consist of various symptoms, decreased food intake, malabsorption, vitamin/mineral deficiencies, osteoporosis, and mechanical problems.
- Careful follow-up with symptomatic/nutritional evaluations, physical exams, and lab tests is critical (Table 61.2).
- Thorough dietary guidance before and after surgery via a specialized dietician is strongly recommended.
- GI tract adaptation varies significantly: some return to normal habits, others need prolonged modifications or jejunostomy tube feeding.

## Dietary Instructions Post-Gastrectomy
- Start with liquid diet, advance to soft postgastrectomy diet as tolerated.
- Eat small, frequent meals (every 2-3 hours), eat slowly, chew food well.
- Include protein, carbs, and fat for adequate calories. Low-sugar protein supplements are encouraged.
- Avoid large volumes of liquids within 30 minutes of meals (reduces early satiety and DS).
- Avoid alcohol, high fat/sugar/insoluble fiber, spicy foods, gas-forming foods, and raw/under-cooked items early on.
- Restrictions gradually relax over 2-3 months based on tolerance.

## Expected Weight Loss
- After subtotal or total gastrectomy, most patients lose **10% to 20%** of their original body weight.
- Primarily due to inadequate food intake (decreased appetite, symptoms).
- Also occurs in patients with adequate caloric intake due to metabolic changes from altered GI hormonal coordination.
- Preoperative counseling regarding postoperative diet and body weight changes is essential.

## Table 61.1: Postgastrectomy Syndromes (Malnutrition & Anemia)

| Syndrome | Pathophysiology | Diagnosis & Treatment Strategies |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Malnutrition/Weight loss** | Loss of appetite (decreased ghrelin), dysphagia, decreased food intake, malabsorption, insufficient digestive enzyme secretion. | Preoperative optimization/counseling. Monitor weight/labs. Small frequent meals, high-protein. Pancreatic enzymes. Multivitamin. |
| **Anemia** | Bypass of duodenum, decreased acid, loss of intrinsic factor (total gastrectomy), folate malabsorption. | Serial labs (hemoglobin, ferritin, iron, B12, MMA). Oral iron, multivitamin. IM/subQ B12 monthly or sublingual B12 daily. |
| **Osteopenia/Osteoporosis** | Bypass of duodenum, pancreatic insufficiency causing vitamin D malabsorption. | Serial labs (calcium, vitamin D). DEXA scan. Vitamin D (3000 IU daily) and calcium citrate (1200-1500 mg daily). |

## Dumping Syndrome (DS): Pathophysiology
- Constellation of GI and vasomotor symptoms postprandially due to rapid emptying of stomach contents into the small intestine.
- Caused by loss of pyloric regulation and/or decreased gastric compliance.
- Unprocessed meal prematurely discharged into proximal small intestine.
- **Early DS:** Occurs <30 min after meal. Hyperosmolar load causes fluid shift into intestinal lumen -> hypovolemia, vascular contraction. Hormones (VIP, serotonin, bradykinin, norepinephrine) mediate response.
- **Late DS:** Occurs 1-3 hours postprandially. Rapid sugar absorption -> acute hyperglycemia -> GLP-1 mediated excessive insulin response -> hypoglycemia.

## Dumping Syndrome: Diagnosis
- Diagnosed mainly by clinical symptoms.
- **Oral glucose challenge:** Fast 10 hrs, ingest 50g glucose. Sensitivity up to 100%, specificity 94%.
- **Scintigraphic gastric emptying study:** Diagnosis verified if >50% of isotope-labeled solid meal empties within 1 hour.
- **Differential Diagnosis:** Gastroparesis, partial small bowel obstruction, anastomotic stricture, postvagotomy diarrhea, IBD, pancreatic insufficiency, bacterial overgrowth.

## Dumping Syndrome: Procedure-Specific Frequencies
- Billroth II reconstruction: Up to 70% of patients.
- Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (obesity): Up to 75%. Late DS in >50%.
- Gastrectomy for cancer: 67% early DS, 38% late DS.
- Sleeve gastrectomy: Low risk of problematic DS (1.6%), but 30-40% have mild symptoms.
- Pyloroplasty/simple GJ: Up to 15%.
- Proximal gastric vagotomy/fundoplication: 2%.
- Roux-en-Y GJ has lower rate (11%) than Billroth I (17%) or Billroth II (70%) due to "duodenal brake".

## Dumping Syndrome: Dietary Treatment
- First-line treatment.
- Small, frequent meals.
- Avoid liquids during and 30 minutes after solid meals.
- High-protein, low-sugar diet; avoid simple carbohydrates.
- Include fiber; lie down 30 mins after meals for vasomotor symptoms.
- Consider high-fat diet for post-vagotomy/post-pyloroplasty DS.
- Eliminate milk/dairy if helpful. Add guar gum/pectin to increase viscosity.
- Hard candy to abort late DS hypoglycemia.

## Dumping Syndrome: Pharmacologic Treatment
- **General symptom meds:** Loperamide (diarrhea), meclizine/promethazine/PPIs (nausea), simethicone (gas).
- **Opium tincture:** Effective for persistent diarrhea.
- **Probiotics:** For gas/bloating from undigested nutrients reaching colon.
- **Anticholinergics (dicyclomine, hyoscyamine):** Slow gastric emptying, antispasmodic.
- **Acarbose:** α-glycosidase inhibitor, delays carb digestion/absorption. Effective for late DS (side effects: flatulence, hypoglycemia).
- **Diazoxide:** Potassium-channel activator, inhibits insulin secretion. For late DS.

## Dumping Syndrome: Octreotide
- Somatostatin analogue for severe, refractory DS.
- Alleviates early and late symptoms by inhibiting hormone mediators.
- Delays gastric emptying and inhibits splanchnic vasodilation.
- Short-acting and long-acting forms equally effective; long-acting better for QOL.
- **Limitations:** Side effects (diarrhea, steatorrhea) and cost lead to noncompliance.

## Dumping Syndrome: Surgical Management
- Only a small percentage require surgery. Do not rush to reoperate.
- Optimize multidisciplinary nonsurgical management first.
- In-hospital observation to verify severity and compliance.
- **Surgical approaches (variable/unpredictable results):**
  - Distal gastrectomy with long-limb Roux-en-Y.
  - "Duodenal switch" (division of postbulbar duodenum + Roux limb).
  - Conversion of Billroth I/II to Roux-en-Y GJ (slows emptying).
  - Reversed intestinal interposition (10-cm reversed segment between stomach and small bowel).

## Figure 61.1: Surgical Approach to Treat Dumping Syndrome
- **Panel A:** Long-limb Roux-en-Y anastomosis. Typical Roux limb is 30-45 cm. A long-limb (jejunojejunostomy created 60 cm from GJ) may alleviate DS and/or alkaline reflux gastritis.
- **Panel B:** Reversed intestinal interposition. A 10-cm loop of jejunum is rotated 180 degrees on its mesentery, positioned in anti-peristaltic fashion between the stomach and proximal small bowel.

## Postvagotomy Diarrhea
- Truncal vagotomy associated with clinically significant diarrhea in 5% to 10% of patients.
- Occurs soon after surgery, usually not associated with other GI/systemic symptoms (distinguishes from dumping).
- Improves over months/years; long-term significant diarrhea in only 1% to 2%.
- **Contributing factors:** Intestinal dysmotility/accelerated transit, bile acid malabsorption, rapid gastric emptying, altered microbiome, bacterial overgrowth.
- **Diagnosis:** Hydrogen breath test for bacterial overgrowth, or empirical trial of oral antibiotics/probiotics.

## Postvagotomy Diarrhea: Management
- **Medical Management:**
  - Cholestyramine (for bile acid malabsorption).
  - Codeine or loperamide.
  - Dietary fiber addition.
  - Patients have >2x the amount of chenodeoxycholic acid in stools, supporting bile acid malabsorption hypothesis.
- **Surgical Management:**
  - Rare, only for debilitated patients unresponsive to medical management for at least 1 year.
  - Surgery of choice: 10-cm reversed jejunal interposition placed 100 cm distal to ligament of Treitz.

## Figure 61.2: Surgical Management of Postvagotomy Diarrhea
- Illustrates a 10-cm loop of jejunum rotated 180 degrees on its mesentery.
- The segment is positioned in an anti-peristaltic fashion.
- Placed 100 cm distal to the pyloroplasty (or ligament of Treitz) to slow transit and treat refractory diarrhea.

## Gastric Stasis: Acute vs. Chronic
- **Acute Gastric Stasis:** Persistent nausea/vomiting prevents NG tube removal. If NG tube needed >7-10 days, place G-tube. Feed via jejunostomy tube or TPN. Delay reoperation for at least 3 months.
- **Chronic Gastric Stasis:** Caused by gastric motor dysfunction (vagal denervation from lesser-curvature lymphadenectomy) or mechanical obstruction.
  - Truncal vagotomy more likely to cause stasis than proximal gastric vagotomy.
  - Obstruction causes: anastomotic stricture, efferent limb kink, constricting mesocolon, retrograde peristalsis in Roux limb.

## Gastric Stasis: Surgical Prevention
- Paramount during distal gastrectomy requiring lesser-curvature (station #1 and #3) lymph node dissection.
- **Remnant size:** A larger remnant (>50%) is more likely to cause stasis. Remove at least 50% of the stomach.
- **Reconstruction:** Antecolic Billroth II with Braun anastomosis, or suture remnant/Roux limb to mesocolon for retrocolic Roux-en-Y.
- This allows gravity to straighten the remnant stomach and facilitate emptying.

## Figure 61.3: The Braun Procedure
- Involves creating a downstream jejuno-jejunostomy to divert bile distally and prevent reflux gastritis.
- A staple line can be added to the afferent limb proximal to the Billroth II GJ ("uncut Roux-en-Y").
- An ante-colic Billroth II anastomosis may be advantageous for optimal gastric emptying and to reduce risk of Roux stasis syndrome.

## Gastric Stasis: Clinical Presentation & Diagnosis
- **Symptoms:** Vomiting (often undigested food), bloating, epigastric pain, weight loss. Improved by liquid diet/fasting.
- **Differential:** Primary gastroparesis, chronic SBO, anastomotic stricture, afferent loop syndrome, internal hernia, GERD, achalasia.
- **Evaluation:**
  - EGD: Gastritis, retained food. Evaluate GJ and efferent limb for stricture.
  - Upper GI series / Gastric emptying scan (scintigraphy).
  - Electrogastrography and GI manometry for motor function disorders.

## Gastric Stasis: Medical Management
- Dietary modification.
- **Promotility agents (Gastrokinetics):**
  - **Metoclopramide:** Dopamine antagonist, facilitates acetylcholine release. Risk of irreversible movement disorder if used >3 months/high doses.
  - **Domperidone:** Facilitates acetylcholine release from mesenteric plexus.
  - **Erythromycin:** Motilin agonist, binds to motilin receptors on GI smooth muscle.
- High-frequency gastric electrical stimulation may be effective for postsurgical gastroparesis refractory to medical therapy (lacking long-term RCTs).

## Gastric Stasis: Surgical Management
- Considered when severe and resistant to medical management.
- **After vagotomy/drainage:** Subtotal (75%) distal gastrectomy. Antecolic Billroth II + Braun enterostomy preferred over Roux-en-Y (to avoid Roux stasis).
- **After subtotal gastric resection:** Near-total (95%) or total gastric resection with Roux-en-Y.
- **Anastomotic stricture/marginal ulcer:** PPI, stop NSAIDs/smoking. Endoscopic dilation.
- **Cancer recurrence:** Multidisciplinary approach; re-resection with caution (often peritoneal metastasis).

## Afferent Loop Obstruction
- Mechanical complication following Billroth II or loop GJ (incidence 0.3%-1.0%).
- Leaves proximal small bowel (duodenum/proximal jejunum) upstream from anastomosis.
- Etiologies:
  1. Entrapment/kinking by adhesions.
  2. Internal herniation, volvulus, intussusception.
  3. Scarring from marginal ulceration.
  4. Locoregional cancer recurrence.
  5. Radiation enteritis.
  6. Enteroliths, bezoars, foreign bodies.
- Redundant afferent loops (>30-40 cm) prone to kinking. Mesenteric defects should be closed (internal hernia incidence up to 22% if not closed).

## Afferent Loop Obstruction: Clinical Presentation
- **Chronic partial obstruction (more common):** Postprandial abdominal pain relieved by bilious vomiting.
  - Meal causes secretions into obstructed limb -> distention -> pressure overcomes obstruction -> bilious vomiting -> pain relief.
  - Weight loss, anemia, bacterial overgrowth (malabsorption of fat, B12, iron).
- **Acute complete obstruction:** Closed loop obstruction, acute abdomen.
  - Nonbilious vomiting, risk of perforation and peritonitis.
  - Urgent surgery required.
- **Physical exam:** Weight loss, upper abdominal distention/mass/tenderness. Jaundice, cholangitis, or pancreatitis may occur.

## Afferent Loop Obstruction: Diagnosis & Treatment
- **CT scan (diagnostic study of choice):**
  - C-shaped, fluid-filled tubular mass between aorta and SMA (C-loop sign).
  - Valvulae conniventes projecting into lumen (keyboard sign).
- **Upper GI contrast study:** Nonfilling or retention of barium in dilated afferent loop (for chronic cases).
- **Treatment (Surgery is cornerstone):**
  - Resection of tumor/ulcer, lysis of adhesions, repair of internal hernia.
  - Addition of Braun anastomosis.
  - Conversion of Billroth II to Roux-en-Y.
  - Revision of Roux-en-Y jejunojejunostomy.
  - Endoscopic/percutaneous interventions (PEG, balloon dilation, stents) for unfit patients or stage IV cancer.

## Figure 61.4: Surgical Management of Afferent Loop Syndrome
- Illustrates three surgical options:
  1. **Conversion to Roux-en-Y:** Altering the anatomy to provide better drainage.
  2. **Excision of the redundant loop:** Removing the kinked or overly long afferent limb.
  3. **Addition of Braun anastomosis:** Creating a downstream jejuno-jejunostomy to bypass the obstruction and drain bile distally.

## Reflux Esophagitis
- Occurs after interruption of antireflux mechanisms (LES, angle of His).
- Acid and/or alkaline intestinal fluid refluxes into lower esophagus.
- Common after total gastrectomy, proximal gastrectomy, and partial gastrectomy involving GE junction.
- Incidence: 10% to 30% after total/proximal gastrectomy.
- Radiation-induced esophagitis can exacerbate symptoms.
- **Symptoms:** Heartburn, dysphagia, chest/back pain, sour taste in mouth. Aspiration can cause chemical pneumonitis.

## Reflux Esophagitis: Surgical Prevention
- **Total Gastrectomy:** Long Roux limb (at least 50-60 cm) decreases incidence. Suture limb to mesocolic defect to prevent sliding herniation.
- **Proximal Gastrectomy:** Mixed-type reflux can be severe.
  - **Jejunal interposition:** Prevents acid reflux, but denervated remnant may delay emptying.
  - **Double-tract reconstruction:** Roux-en-Y + side-to-side anastomosis between Roux limb and gastric remnant. KLASS-05 RCT showed safety, decreased reflux, improved QOL vs total gastrectomy.
  - **Double-flap technique & Side overlap with fundoplication (Yamashita):** Create antireflux mechanism. Efficacy in Western patients unknown.

## Reflux Esophagitis: Medical & Surgical Treatment
- **Medical/Dietary:**
  - Avoid large portions/high-fat meals.
  - Finish dinner 2-3 hours before bed. Sleep with 45-60 degree head elevation (Fowler position).
  - Acid-dominant: Antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers.
  - Alkaline-dominant: Cholestyramine, camostat mesylate, mucosa-protective antiacids.
  - Promotility agents (metoclopramide, erythromycin) to empty Roux limb.
- **Surgical (for persistent >1 year severe symptoms):**
  - Modify jejunojejunostomy to make Roux limb longer (>60 cm; up to 150 cm for bariatric).
  - Repair hiatal hernia.
  - Staple redundant blind end of Roux limb.

## Figure 61.5: Roux-en-Y Reconstruction After Total Gastrectomy
- Illustrates the anatomy following total gastrectomy.
- Typical length of the Roux-limb is at least **50-60 cm**.
- For bariatric patients, the limb is lengthened to prevent and/or manage reflux esophagitis.

## Alkaline (Bile) Reflux Gastritis
- Caused by longstanding presence of abnormal amount of duodenal content in gastric remnant.
- Common after pyloroplasty or loop GJ.
- **Histologic bile gastritis:** Present in up to 85% of Billroth II patients, mostly asymptomatic. More common than Billroth I (29-48%) or drainage ops (15%).
- Role of gastric acid is unclear; acid potentiates mucosal damage from bile salts but inactivates pancreatic enzymes.
- Can lead to dysplasia and gastric "stump" cancer.
- **Clinical bile gastritis:** Symptoms include abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, weight loss, anemia.

## Alkaline Reflux Gastritis: Diagnosis
- Largely based on symptoms and endoscopy.
- **Endoscopy:** Inflammatory changes extending beyond peristomal area suggest excessive enterogastric reflux.
- **Histology:** Foveolar hyperplasia, glandular cystic degeneration, edema of lamina propria, vasocongestion of mucosal capillaries, minimal inflammatory cell infiltration.
- Endoscopic/histologic features do **not** correlate well with symptom severity.
- Abdominal CT useful to exclude other causes.

## Alkaline Reflux Gastritis: Medical Treatment
- Cholestyramine.
- Antacids.
- H2 blockers.
- PPIs.
- Sucralfate.
- Promotility agents to enhance clearance of refluxate from gastric remnant.

## Alkaline Reflux Gastritis: Surgical Treatment
- Considered for incapacitating symptoms, secure diagnosis, realistic expectations.
- Aim: Divert duodenal contents away from stomach.
- **Roux-en-Y GJ (most frequent):** 60-cm Roux limb reliably diverts contents. Improves symptoms in up to 85% of patients. Epigastric pain recurs in up to 30% long-term.
- **Henley operation:** Isoperistaltic jejunal loop (40 cm) interposed between remnant and duodenum. Satisfactory in 70%, but less technically simple.
- **Duodenal switch (suprapapillary duodenojejunostomy):** Roux-en-Y without gastrectomy. Good results for primary bile reflux or alkaline gastritis after pyloroplasty.
- Pre/postoperative nutritional support and jejunostomy tube placement should be considered.

## Figure 61.6: Duodenal Switch Procedure
- As described by DeMeester et al. for primary bile or alkaline reflux gastritis after pyloroplasty.
- The postbulbar duodenum is divided.
- A 60-cm retrocolic Roux limb is anastomosed to the proximal duodenum to divert bile away from the stomach without altering gastric emptying.

## Roux Stasis Syndrome
- Attributed to measurable abnormalities in Roux limb motility (delayed emptying) after gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y.
- Abnormal peristalsis: Propulsive contractile waves proceeding proximally (toward stomach/esophagus).
- **Etiology:** Transection of jejunum creates ectopic pacemaker, causing dysmotility and slow transit.
- More common with large gastric remnant or after vagotomy.
- Quite uncommon after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (small pouch) or cancer gastrectomy (small remnant).

## Roux Stasis Syndrome: Diagnosis
- **Symptoms:** Abdominal pain, distention, postprandial bloating, nausea, vomiting (solid food, nonbilious).
- Bacterial overgrowth with diarrhea and nutrient malabsorption may result.
- **Endoscopy:** Dilated gastric remnant, retained food, mucosal irritation. Patent anastomosis, dilated Roux limb.
- **CT/Upper GI:** No mechanical obstruction.
- **Scintigraphy:** Markedly delayed emptying of solids. Liquid emptying usually normal.

## Roux Stasis Syndrome: Medical & Surgical Treatment
- **Medical:** Dietary adjustments, prokinetic agents. Intestinal/stomach pacing investigated but unproven.
- **Surgical (for debilitating symptoms):**
  - If original gastrectomy removed <50%: Subtotal gastrectomy with new Roux limb (resect original) OR Billroth II with Braun enteroenterostomy.
  - "Uncut Roux" procedure (TA staple line in afferent limb) preserves motility but staple line opens up transiently.
  - If original gastrectomy removed >50%: Total/near-total (95%) gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y.
  - Limit Roux limb to 50 cm in revisional operations to reduce stasis risk.
  - Add feeding jejunostomy.

## Marginal Ulcers
- Juxtaanastomotic ulceration after GJ anastomosis.
- Incidence: 0.6% to 25%. More common after Roux-en-Y than Billroth II (lacks afferent limb buffering).
- Usually on jejunal side of anastomosis.
- **Contributing factors:** Chronic ischemia, smoking, NSAIDs, alcohol, permanent suture material, incomplete vagotomy, H. pylori, hypergastrinemia.
- **Presentation:** Acute (perforation) or chronic. Abdominal pain, vomiting, chronic/acute blood loss.

## Marginal Ulcers: Treatment
- **Medical:** PPIs, antibiotics for H. pylori, eliminate NSAIDs, smoking cessation. Misoprostol, Carafate.
- **Surgical (if medical fails):**
  - Thoracoscopic truncal vagotomy (if incomplete vagotomy diagnosed via sham-feeding pancreatic polypeptide test).
  - Reexcision (if retained antrum confirmed via operative/pathology reports or technetium-99m scan). G cells in retained antral tissue secrete gastrin continuously, causing high acid.
  - Rule out gastrinoma (pancreas).
  - Revisional GJ or esophagojejunostomy for persistent ulcers.

## Gallstones: Pathophysiology
- Gallstone formation occurs in 10% to 20% of patients, typically within 3 years.
- **Vagal denervation:** Results in gallbladder dysmotility (from lesser curve lymphadenectomy, truncal vagotomy, or division of hepatic branches of left vagal nerve).
- Higher risk and earlier occurrence after total gastrectomy and extended lymphadenectomy.
- **Exclusion of duodenum:** Roux-en-Y decreases cholecystokinin (CCK) secretion, decreasing gallbladder motility.
- **Other factors:** Weight loss (mobilizes cholesterol, supersaturates bile), edema/inflammation around bile ducts (biliary stasis).

## Gallstones: Risk by Procedure & Management
- After gastrectomy for cancer: 25% develop stones within 2 years, 6% undergo cholecystectomy.
- More likely after radical gastrectomy (30%) than simple (5%).
- Roux-en-Y increases risk vs. techniques preserving duodenal passage (28%).
- Gastric bypass: 5.8x risk in first 2 years. Intrinsically more lithogenic than adjustable gastric banding.
- **Management:** No consensus on prophylactic cholecystectomy. Routine cholecystectomy at gastrectomy is **not** recommended.
- Consider cholecystectomy if sludge/stones/abnormal gallbladder found intraoperatively, especially if subsequent cholecystectomy would be difficult.

## Nutritional Abnormalities: General Overview
- Caused by loss of gastric volume, impaired ghrelin, altered GI tract (duodenum bypass), and general postgastrectomy symptoms.
- Results in decreased caloric intake and malabsorption of protein, fat, vitamins, iron, calcium, and minerals.
- Deficiencies develop months to years after gastrectomy.
- **Management:** Systematic monitoring (Table 61.2), small frequent meals, multivitamin (iron, folate, selenium, copper, zinc, vit A, vit E).
- Calcium citrate with vitamin D (1500 mg daily). B12 supplementation (1000 mcg IM monthly or 350-500 mcg sublingual daily).

## Weight Loss After Gastrectomy
- Typically 10% to 20% of preoperative body weight.
- **Causes:**
  1. Altered dietary intake (loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, pain, self-imposed modifications).
  2. Malabsorption (bacterial overgrowth in "blind loops", decreased absorptive surface area from resection/Roux limb).
- Fat malabsorption causes diarrhea/malnutrition (acid inactivates pancreatic enzymes, poor mixing, bacterial overgrowth).
- **Diagnosis/Treatment:** Qualitative test for fecal fat, decreased fat-soluble vitamins. Treat with pancreatic enzyme supplements and oral antibiotics (for bacterial overgrowth). Consult dietitian. Prolonged enteral/parenteral nutrition may be necessary.

## Anemia After Gastrectomy
- Occurs in up to one-third of patients.
- Caused by nutrient malabsorption, decreased intake, or chronic blood loss.
- **Iron deficiency (most common):** Absorption primarily in duodenum/proximal jejunum, facilitated by acidic environment.
- **Vitamin B12 deficiency:** Loss of intrinsic factor (made by parietal cells), facilitated by acidic environment. Life-threatening after total gastrectomy without supplementation.
- **Folate deficiency:** Folate-rich foods (leafy greens, fruit) may be problematic for small/hypomotile pouch.
- **Treatment:** Monitor all patients for these three deficiencies. Supplement orally (iron, folate) and IM/sublingual (B12).

## Chronic Calcium Deficits and Osteoporosis
- Increased risk due to decreased oral intake, malabsorption of calcium/vitamin D, absence of stomach acid, lack of gastrocalcin.
- Calcium absorbed primarily in duodenum; bypassed by loop GJ, Billroth II, Roux-en-Y, or obesity bypass.
- Inadequate mixing of food/enzymes and bacterial overgrowth interfere with fat-soluble vitamin (D) absorption.
- **Management:**
  - Annual monitoring of calcium and vitamin D levels. Supplement both.
  - Routine DEXA scan every 2 years for low BMI, significant weight loss, or risk factors (age >50 women, >65 men, history of fracture/smoking).
  - Identify early, reversible skeletal deterioration.
